title: 3 kinds of conflict at work (and why naming it matters)
caption:
You can't fix a conflict you've misnamed.

Most workplace conflict is one of three kinds:

1. Task: we disagree about the work itself.
2. Relationship: there's friction between us.
3. Process: nobody is clear on who does what, or who decides.

Here's the part most teams miss. Process problems get treated like personality problems. "She's difficult" is often "nobody decided who owns this."

Which one is your team in right now? Tell me below.
notes: 5 slides. 1: You can't fix a conflict you've misnamed. 2: Task: disagreement about the work itself. 3: Relationship: friction between people. 4: Process: who does what, and who decides. 5: Which one is your team in? Cream background, rust headings.

title: Quote: "She is difficult" is often "nobody decided who owns this."
caption:
Before you decide it's a people problem, check whether it's a process problem.

Unclear roles feel personal. They usually aren't.

Save this for the next time a coworker is "being difficult."
notes: Single quote card, espresso background, cream text, gold rule.

title: Face slot: Why I teach conflict
caption:
Most of us were never taught how to handle conflict. We learned it by watching, and what we watched was silence, blowups, or both.

I teach conflict resolution to college students every week. The same skills change how a team works.

Something new is coming for teams that carry heavy work. More soon.

title: The two-day email test
caption:
Your coworker hasn't replied to your email in two days.

Quick: why?

Whatever you just answered is a story. Psychologists call it an attribution, and it decides what you do next.

We tend to explain other people by their character ("she's ignoring me") and ourselves by our situation ("I was slammed").

Before you react, come up with two other explanations that fit the same facts.

What was your first answer? Be honest.
notes: 15-second text reel, ready to post. Add a trending or calm audio track in Instagram.

title: Say this instead: reframing
caption:
Same frustration, two very different conversations.

Instead of: "You never listen to me."
Try: "I don't feel like I'm getting through when we talk about this. Can we start over?"

Reframing means saying what you need without attacking the person. It isn't being soft. It's being heard.

What's a line you wish you could take back?
notes: Split card. Top (rust outline): Instead of: You never listen to me. Bottom (sage fill): Try: I don't feel like I'm getting through when we talk about this. Can we start over?

title: 3 patterns that escalate conflict
caption:
Escalation isn't random. It usually follows one of three patterns.

1. Demand-withdraw: one person pushes, the other retreats, and both dig in.
2. Contempt: sarcasm, eye-rolling, a tone that says "I'm above you."
3. Stonewalling: shutting down completely. It usually comes from overwhelm, even though it looks like not caring.

Once you can see the pattern, you can interrupt it.

Which one do you reach for under pressure?
notes: 5 slides. 1: Conflict escalates in patterns. 2: Demand-withdraw. 3: Contempt. 4: Stonewalling. 5: Which one is yours? Espresso background for slide 1, cream for the rest.

title: Story poll: Under pressure, I usually...
notes: Add a poll or quiz sticker to story 1 with the options: Push harder / Go quiet / Get sarcastic / Stay steady. Post story 2 right after.

title: Quote: A break with a return time
caption:
Needing a minute is not the problem.

A break with a return time is regulation.
A break without one is stonewalling.

"I need twenty minutes. Can we pick this up at 2?" is a complete, professional sentence.
notes: Quote card, cream background: A break with a return time is regulation. A break without one is stonewalling.

caption:

title: Quote: The skill is choosing
caption:
Competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating.

None of them is the right one. Each fits some moments and fails in others.

Most of us have one default we use whether it fits or not. The skill is choosing.

What's your default?
notes: Quote card, espresso background: No style is the right one. The skill is choosing.
